scenario: A 30-year-old G1P0 patient at 35 weeks gestational age presents with worsening shortness of breath and severe asthma exacerbation in pregnancy, initially hypoxic on room air and requiring stepwise respiratory support and asthma therapy.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Start her on high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather now—she's satting 85% on room air with a rate of 32.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Non-rebreather is on and running.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: The oxygen's helping, but your breathing's still fast. Tell me what's going on right now and when did the trouble breathing start—did it come on suddenly or build up over time?

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: I can't breathe right — I'm wheezing and I've had this dry cough for about a week now. It didn't hit me all at once, it just kept getting worse and worse over time. I had a fever for three days but that's gone now. And I ran out of my salbutamol inhaler, so there's nothing to help.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Let's get a salbutamol nebulizer going now for her wheezing.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: I'm setting you up with a salbutamol nebulizer now for your breathing. Keep it over your nose and mouth and breathe normally through it.

patient_emotion.notes: [nurse: I'm setting you up with a salbutamol nebulizer now for your breathing. Keep it over your nose and mouth and breathe normally through it.] This utterance is routine, reassuring care delivery with clear simple instructions for a treatment the patient already knows helps. Fear stays absent - this is a calm, concrete step addressing the very symptom relief the patient lacked (out of salbutamol), not a threat disclosure. Sadness stays absent - no loss conveyed. Overwhelm stays absent - single simple instruction, not information overload. Shame stays absent - supportive, nonjudgmental tone.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: Fine, give it here — I'll breathe through it. But I'm still wheezing and can't catch my breath, I'm having to fight for every breath.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Give IV methylprednisolone now for her ongoing wheezing despite the neb.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: I'm ordering a chest X-ray to look for infection, since you've had a week of cough and a recent fever. And running out of your inhaler is a big part of why you ended up this sick. Before we give you anything more—do you have any allergies to medications?

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: I'm ordering a chest X-ray to look for infection, since you've had a week of cough and a recent fever. messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: No, I don't have any allergies to medications. Now can we get on with it — I still can't breathe.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Add ipratropium to the nebulizer now—she's still wheezing and working hard despite the salbutamol.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Ipratropium is in and running now.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: I'm getting a chest X-ray to check for pneumonia, given the week of cough and your recent fever. Your oxygen level is good now, but you're still breathing fast, so we're keeping the treatment going. Do you have any past lung problems or other medical conditions I should know about?

messages.content: Chest X-ray is back: prominent vascular markings, normal in pregnancy; normal cardiomediastinal contour; lungs and pleural spaces clear. No consolidation or infiltrate. Vitals now HR 107, BP 99/59, RR 20, SpO2 98% on NRB at FiO2 0.8.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: Yes — I've got asthma, it flares up with colds and anything that irritates my lungs. I was intubated once for an attack when I was a kid, around eleven. About a year ago I was in the ED and had to take steroid pills. And I'm 35 weeks pregnant. I normally use a budesonide inhaler and my prenatal vitamins. And I'm still fighting for every breath here.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Give IV magnesium sulfate now—she's still working hard despite the nebs and steroids. It's safe at 35 weeks.
